article_title: The 3 Phases of the AI Layer Most Services-as-Software Founders Get Wrong

text:
i regret to inform you that the ai agents you've been building are not the part that does the work.

the data layer underneath is the work.

the agents are just the wrapper.

here's the right way to do it: https://t.co/drpiYgRZwx

I've sent 23,000,000+ cold emails (and these are the only 100 tips that matter).

Bookmark this.

Deliverability

1. Deliverability is the foundation. Without it, the best copy lands in spam.
2. Your primary domain is sacred. Cold sends go from alternates only.
3. Buy alternate domains. Forward them to your main site.
4. SPF, DKIM, DMARC. Set them before the first send or you've already lost.
5. Warm inboxes before the first send. No shortcuts.
6. Cap each inbox at a safe daily volume. Above that, you cook deliverability.
7. Scale by adding inboxes, not by cranking volume per address.
8. One Google Workspace caps you at a handful of inboxes. Stack workspaces.
9. Microsoft inboxes aren't cold-outreach infrastructure. They flag and burn.
10. Check domain reputation weekly. Catch issues before they cook your sender score.

Infrastructure & Inbox Setup

11. Alternate domains should mirror your main domain.
12. Forward alternates to your real site. Never to a parking page.
13. Auto-warm before the first send. Instantly, Smartlead, and Lemlist all have it built in.
14. Verify every address. Bounces tank reputation faster than anything else.
15. Run a fresh verification pass on every list. Don't trust "pre-verified" data. Verification ages out.
16. Rotate inboxes inside each campaign. Don't blast from one address.
17. Stagger sends across business hours. No single-spike sending.
18. Include an unsubscribe link even if you don't legally have to. Signals legitimacy.
19. Plaintext beats HTML. No images, no fancy formatting.
20. Tracking pixels kill deliverability. Turn them off.

List Quality

21. A list of right-fit accounts beats a list of spray-and-pray.
22. ICP first. If you can't describe your buyer in one sentence, you don't have one.
23. Stack signals. One signal is a guess. Three or more is intent.
24. Job changes, hiring posts, funding rounds, tech stack moves. Those are buying triggers.
25. Title match isn't enough. A "VP Marketing" at a small agency is a different buyer than at a large SaaS.
26. Buy data from Apollo or ZoomInfo. Verify it in Clay.
27. Scrape engagement on competitors with Trigify. People who liked their posts are warm to your offer.
28. Triangulate from two sources before sending. Single-source lists are dirty.
29. Suppress customers, lost deals, and competitors. Suppression lists matter.
30. Re-pull lists regularly. Data goes stale fast.

Personalization

31. Relevance is the unlock. Personalization without relevance is decoration.
32. Personalize the reason for reaching out, not the opener.
33. Skip the icebreaker. "Hope you're doing well" buys you nothing.
34. Reference something the prospect did. Not their LinkedIn About section.
35. AI personalization works when grounded in a real signal. Garbage in, garbage out.
36. Feed AI a real input: a job post, a podcast clip, a tweet. Then the line lands.
37. Don't fake personalization. Prospects clock a template instantly.
38. One specific detail beats three vague ones.
39. If you can't say something genuinely relevant, skip the slot.
40. Test personalized against sharp generic. Sometimes generic wins.

Subject Lines

41. Subject lines are the first filter. Get past the preview or nothing else matters.
42. Lowercase looks human. Title Case looks corporate.
43. Keep them short. A handful of words at most.
44. "Quick question," "intro," "{{firstName}}." All overused. Skip.
45. Personal works: "saw the {company} hiring post"
46. Don't use the prospect's first name in the subject. Triggers spam classifiers.
47. No emojis. No question marks at the end. No ALL CAPS.
48. A/B test the angle, not the adjectives. Big swings move open rate; tweaks don't.
49. Match subject to body. Bait-and-switch tanks reply rate.
50. The best subject is one that doesn't sound like a sales pitch.

Body Copy

51. Keep first-touch copy short. Long messages don't get read.
52. Mobile is the default. Most cold outreach opens on phone first.
53. A few sentences max. One paragraph. White space matters.
54. Lead with the reason you're reaching out. Not who you are.
55. Don't introduce yourself in the first line. They don't care yet.
56. State the trigger. State the relevance. Ask.
57. Drop "I came across your profile and was impressed by." Nobody talks like that.
58. Strip the closer's adjectives: innovative, synergize, best-in-class.
59. Write like a Slack DM. Not a press release.
60. One idea per send. Stack three benefits and you get zero replies.

The Ask

61. One ask per send. Not two. Never three.
62. Soft asks beat hard asks on first touch. Ask for interest, not a calendar slot.
63. Yes/no questions force a reply. "Are you the right person for this?" works.
64. "Want me to send over the breakdown?" is one of the highest-converting asks we've seen.
65. Calendar links on first touch kill reply rates. Save them for later in the cadence.
66. Avoid "let me know if you'd like to learn more." Passive asks get passive responses.
67. Frame the ask around the prospect's benefit, not yours.
68. PS lines work. Drop your strongest proof point there.
69. Never include two links. Each extra link drags response down.
70. The ask isn't where you sell. It's where you make replying easy.

Sequences & Follow-Ups

71. Multi-touch sequences win. Most replies arrive on the later touches, not the first.
72. Space follow-ups a few business days apart. Daily is aggressive without being useful.
73. Each follow-up adds value. New angle, new asset, new question. Not just a re-poke.
74. The "did this get buried?" bump works exactly once.
75. Reference the prior message in the follow-up. Reply chains build context.
76. Vary structure across the cadence. Long, short, question, asset, breakup.
77. The breakup isn't a sad note. It's a final useful nudge.
78. Don't send a breakup if you don't want to break up. Recycle the lead later.
79. Multi-channel sequences outperform single-channel. Add LinkedIn and phone to the cadence.
80. Hand off replies to humans immediately. Auto-responses to replies kill trust.

Reply Handling

81. Respond to replies fast. Speed signals seriousness.
82. Don't sell on the reply. Confirm interest, then book the call.
83. Suggest a couple of specific time windows. Don't just paste a Calendly link.
84. Send a one-line agenda before the call. Cuts no-shows materially.
85. Confirm the day before. Confirm again the hour before for high-value prospects.
86. If they ghost after booking, send one reminder. Then move on.
87. "Not now" isn't "no." Tag and set a reminder for later in the quarter.
88. "Wrong person" replies are gold. Always ask for the intro.
89. Negative replies often convert later. Don't argue. Thank them and exit gracefully.
90. Track reply sentiment, not just reply rate. Positive replies are the only metric that matters.

Mistakes That Tank Pipeline

91. More volume is never the answer when reply rate is low. Fix the input.
92. Don't add SDRs before the system works. You'll just multiply broken output.
93. Don't fix copy when targeting is broken. Targeting is the majority of outcomes.
94. Don't fix targeting when deliverability is broken. Nothing else matters if you're in spam.
95. Don't blame the channel. Cold outreach isn't dead. Bad cold outreach is.
96. Stop optimizing open rate. Optimize for booked calls and closed pipeline.
97. Don't trust "industry benchmarks." Your numbers depend on your ICP, offer, and seniority.
98. Don't run a campaign without a hypothesis. "Let's see what happens" is not a strategy.
99. Don't measure cold outreach in isolation. It works as a layer in a broader GTM system.
100. Don't outsource cold outreach without owning the strategy. The agency should run the playbook. And you should be involved in writing the playbook.

text:
if your pipeline isn't growing and you think it's because one channel is failing or underperforming, stop. read this before you move that budget to a new channel.

oftentimes the channel is doing its job. the real issue is one of the five layers every channel depends on.

here's how to build your GTM system so pipeline grows predictably:

1/ foundation

everything that has to be true before you spend a dollar on any channel.

can you quote a real buyer describing their problem in their own words? if not, your messaging is a guess, and a channel doesn't fix a guess. it just delivers it to more people. we pull those exact phrases from sales call recordings.

the inbox matters just as much: gmail now rejects unauthenticated bulk mail outright. if open rates dropped and the copy didn't change, check SPF, DKIM and DMARC before you touch a subject line.

2/ strategy

most teams run one channel until it has a bad quarter, then call it dead. every channel has a bad quarter eventually, and when it's the only one you run, that quarter looks like the end.

we run three that cover for each other: content warms people up, ads keep us in front of them, outbound starts the conversations. that shift alone took us from $40K to $90K a month.

3/ execution

the channels themselves, where everyone starts and where most budgets get wasted.

the most common version: paying for ads to reach strangers while the audience your content already earned sits there untouched.

we get 100+ inbound meetings a month from linkedin without spending a dollar on ads, and the same people who read that content get our cold emails. by the time we show up in their inbox, they already know who we are.

4/ compounding

most replies arrive on the later touches, but most teams stop following up long before that, look at the thin results, and conclude the channel stopped working.

the follow-up is only half of this layer. the other half is what you count: meetings booked is a vanity metric any tool can inflate. pipeline created and revenue closed live in your CRM, and those are the numbers the business actually runs on.

5/ learning

every tactic decays eventually. the teams that survive it sit down once a week and close the loop: which signal converted, which message landed, which channel paid for itself.

the teams that skip this keep running the same play long after it stopped working, and when results dry up, the channel gets the blame. sound familiar?

find your broken layer:

> replies fine, revenue flat = layer 4
> one great month, then two dead ones = layer 1
> everything works a little, nothing compounds = layer 2
> open rates dropped, copy didn't change = layer 1, the inbox
> busy team, nobody knows what worked = layer 5

fix the lowest broken layer first.

if pipeline feels random, start at layer 1.

one of the domains in your cold email setup is carrying other people's spam complaints.

it's the tracking domain, and your own reporting will never show it.

the shared tracking domain your sending platform hands you by default sits on every other customer's links too, so their spam complaints ride into your emails on the same wrapper. your own sending looks clean the whole time.

that's step 4 of 8.

@Kenny_GTM sets up the cold email infrastructure on every client account we run. we've sent 23M+ cold emails across those campaigns. here's his full build order:

1/ domains

buy 10 to 15 for a launch build, 20 for the full spec, all close variations of your brand. keep the primary domain out of the sending path.

burning a sending domain is routine and survivable. burning the one your contracts and invoices go through means you spend months repairing your company's email rather than a campaign.

2/ mailboxes

run 2 or 3 per domain and never more. past that the domain reads as a sending farm.

split the estate 50/50 between google workspace and microsoft 365, because the two filter on different rules. put everything on one provider and one bad filtering week hits all of your capacity instead of half of it.

3/ dns

SPF, DKIM and DMARC go on every domain before any mailbox sends, warm-up included.

weak copy costs you reply rate over weeks. a domain with no authentication gets flagged on the first send, before anyone opens the email. you read it as a bounce rate that stays high no matter what you change in the copy.

4/ tracking domain

the one from the top of this post. teams skip it more than any other step, and skipping it undoes steps 1 through 3.

one subdomain you own, configured per sending account.

5/ platform

instantly handles pure email. lemlist earns its place when linkedin matters. smartlead comes in when the client brings it.

connect every mailbox before warm-up so the platform builds the sending history for you.

6/ rotation and warm-up

mailbox rotation goes on from day one so sends spread across the estate. every mailbox then gets 2 weeks minimum before it touches a campaign, and 30 days is the safer number now that gmail puts a warning banner on domains younger than that.

cut it short and the failure only surfaces after the campaign is live and the domain is already marked, and warm-up won't repair it from there. you replace the domain and start over.

7/ send limits

cap each mailbox at 20 to 25 sends a day. volume comes from mailbox count.

40 mailboxes at that rate sends 800 to 1,000 a day and none of them looks unusual. set the cap inside the platform itself.

8/ placement

clear 95%+ in the primary inbox before the first real campaign. anything sitting in spam produces no pipeline at all.

if you're running this spec and landing well under 95%, the cause is back in steps 1 through 6.

domains get replaced every 9 to 12 months. stagger the replacements, because rotating all 20 at once puts the whole estate back to zero and every new domain still owes you its two weeks of warm-up.

the two numbers that break first:

> spam rate above 0.1%
> bounce rate above 3%

both shift weeks before reply rate does. by the time reply rate drops, the damage is a few weeks old and the domain is usually past repairing.

all of that is phase 1. phase 2 is data and targeting, phase 3 is the copy.

most teams start at phase 3 in week 1, which is why they spend the next month debugging subject lines for a domain problem.

you just read phase 1. @Kenny_GTM wrote all three, plus the ten-line weekly dashboard and the numbers that mean you already have a problem.

article_title: How to Pick the Right Claude Model

text: Going live in 45min to show you how to do GTM Engineering like the top 1%

if AI looks expensive in your outbound, look at what you're running opus on.

most of a campaign isn't thinking work. it's lookups, filters, checks and dedupes. a frontier model doesn't do any of that better than a script does, it just costs more and adds variance to an answer that was never in question.

so price the step before you hand it to anything. two things decide it:

how open-ended is the work?
how far does a bad output get before someone catches it?

then give it to the cheapest thing that clears both, which is somewhere between a plain python script and a person.

here's where the 7 steps of an outbound campaign sit:

1/ qualifying against your ICP
a python script. no model in the loop, $0. it applies a firmographic floor, scores the signal, and buckets the account. run the same account through it twice and you get the same answer twice, which is the whole reason it isn't a model.

2/ suppression and preflight
claude code hooks, also $0. an account already sitting in an open sequence doesn't get put in a second one, spend caps hold, send windows run on the account's own timezone so nothing shows up at 6am local and gets read as spam. none of that is a judgment call.

3/ signal feeds and list pulls
haiku 4.5, the 1x baseline. 10,000 rows a pull, filtered down to the ones that moved. it needs a model at all because a hiring post and a repost of someone else's hiring post look nearly the same in plain text.

4/ account research and tiering
sonnet 5, roughly 3x. reads the account, interprets the signal, then maps who signs, who evaluates, and who uses it daily. this used to be affordable on the top 20% of a list. it runs on the whole list now, for less than that top slice cost.

5/ QA in front of every send
sonnet 5 again. three checks on every message before it goes out: ICP fit, the claims it makes, tone.

6/ first-draft copy and strategy
opus 5, and fable 5 when the reasoning gets hard. 5x to 10x. this is the one step that earns it. a weak draft here travels into every account on the list.

7/ picking the signal, approving the send
a person, which is the most expensive tier in the stack and is supposed to be. on a 500 account campaign we look at about 50 at the front and read about 50 sends at the back. the other 400 move through steps 1 to 6 without anyone touching them.

i had this backwards for a long time, and i don't think the instinct is stupid. nobody wants to be the person who under-provisioned a step and shipped something bad. so the frontier model ends up running everything.

The problem is that distribution isn't a tool. It's 7 jobs that feed each other, and if you run them out of order it doesn't matter what you bought.

Here's what each job does, in the order they have to run:

1/ Signal
You want to know the moment something moves at an account, whether that's a funding round, a new VP in the buyer's seat, or a hiring spike, and you want it arriving with a note on why it fired. Hold onto that note, it comes back in step 6.

2/ List on demand
When a signal fires you enrich that one account right then, instead of paying upfront for twelve months of records you might never open.

3/ Score and tier
You score every account on six weighted factors, and each one has to be checkable from the outside before anyone talks to you. Nobody finishes this layer, because what it ends up telling you is to stop calling most of your list, and nobody wants to hear that. Finish it anyway.

4/ Channel routing
The tier decides which channel an account gets before anyone opens an inbox, and tier 1 always gets an actual person. A signal can bump an account up one tier, never two, no matter how good it looks.

5/ Content
You post enough that people have heard of you before the email lands, and anyone who engages goes straight back into step 1 as a signal.

6/ Outbound
Remember the note from step 1? It becomes the opener here. If an account has no note on file, it doesn't get sent at all.

7/ Feedback loop
Everything writes back into the same table, the replies, the deals that died, the no-shows. And keep the no-shows, seriously. Those people booked a meeting with you, they were just early.

Running it in this order took us from 1 deal per 1,000 cold emails to 3, out of the same inboxes, without adding a single send.

text:
Found a 22-year-old clip of Peter Thiel and Max Levchin breaking distribution down to what each customer cost PayPal.

In September 1999 PayPal was 22 people, and Silicon Valley had two main ways to get customers.

The first was advertising. A billboard on the highway into San Francisco went from $10K a month in '97 to $100K a month in '99, and drivers got 6 to 10 seconds to read it.

The second was a big partner. They flew to London to pitch HSBC, and the executives told them about the TV ads they had just started running.

So PayPal started paying people to join. 

$10 to open an account and another $10 for every friend they brought in. People called it the most insane scheme of all time. It worked out to $20 a customer, and the next cheapest option was online ads at about $65.

Then eBay sellers started asking to put PayPal's logo on their auctions. PayPal told them no for two months, until it noticed they were joining without the $20.

In 2014 Thiel put the same math into the distribution chapter of Zero to One. The profit you make over a customer's lifetime decides what you can spend to win a customer, and that decides which channel you can afford.

Here's how he lays it out, from the biggest deals down:

1/ Seven figures and up. The founder sells. Palantir's CEO was on the road 25 days a month.

2/ $10K to $100K. A small sales team runs a process it can repeat.

3/ Around $1,000 a year for small-business software. The dead zone. The buyer still needs a conversation, and the price can't cover a salesperson's time.

4/ Low price with mass appeal. Advertising, when other channels are uneconomical.

5/ Viral. The product brings in the next user, the way a PayPal payment could.

PayPal priced its options and went with the cheapest one. Thiel's line on it in the book: "If you can get just one distribution channel to work, you have a great business."

text:
AI only gives you something good when the system under it is right and the data going in is right.

Before you let AI take over your cold email, make sure you do these seven things (below) first. You'll thank me later.

1/ Stop sending to bought lists.

About a quarter of a bought list is dead within a year, and every dead address is a bounce that hurts your domain. Build the list from live sources and keep bounces under 2%.

2/ Score every account for fit before anyone writes to it.

Fit is the company, the role, and the tools they already use. Timing is what changed at that company in the last two weeks. Keep them as two separate scores.

3/ Verify every email with more than one provider.

One provider finds about half the emails. Three in sequence got us to 85 to 90%. For your best accounts, open the LinkedIn profile as well. A verified email only proves the mailbox exists, and people who left last quarter still show up as verified.

4/ Only send when something just changed at the account.

A new VP 12 days ago, a pricing page changed 5 days ago. "They're hiring" is always true, so it never tells you when to send. We track 70 of these signals and send inside 14 days of the change. This is where the reply rate moves.

5/ Let AI write the reason you're reaching out, then read it before it goes.

The agent reads the company's site, news, and job posts and writes one line. Tell it to return "SKIP" when nothing changed in the last 14 days, or it will find a reason for every account. A human reads every message before it leaves.

6/ Run one campaign per account at a time.

Two campaigns on the same account and you lose track of which one earned the reply. Your best accounts get email, LinkedIn, and a call. The next tier gets email and LinkedIn. Everyone else gets email.

7/ Feed what closed back into the list.

Every quarter, take the last 30 to 50 deals you won, pull the company domains, and score the next list against them. All of them paid you and stayed.

Most teams we audit get to step 3 and stop. Clean, scored, verified list, then they send it on a Tuesday. Instantly's 2026 benchmark puts the average cold email reply at 3.43%. Our signal-based campaigns get 5 to 18% on the same AI models.

The full build for each step is in the article (bookmark for later).

If you're a founder or running GTM, build one account list your whole growth engine can use.

Start with your 10 best customers. Put their domains into AI Ark's lookalike search, find similar companies, and pull 2 to 3 buyers per account. Verify their emails and fill the gaps with Prospeo.

Keep the company domain, segment, buying trigger, outreach tier and status together in Clay. That record should tell the next tool who the account is and what's already happened.

Then build the campaign around it:

→ Outbound: tier accounts by segment fit and a live buying trigger. Accounts with both get email, LinkedIn and a call from your team. Those with either one get email and LinkedIn. Keep broader-fit accounts with neither on email.

→ Paid: use the company list for LinkedIn ads and Vibe’s streaming TV ads. Match the data to each platform's requirements. Google Customer Match needs first-party contacts. Keep the offer consistent as you adapt the creative.

→ Search and landing pages: answer the questions buyers ask about pricing, alternatives and how the work gets done. Give each segment a page with a clear promise, proof and next action. Use the same brief for the page, ads and outreach.

→ Workflows: build a workflow that connects reply events across your tools. When someone responds, have it stop their other sequences, update the CRM and write the result back to the account. Add a monthly refresh to re-verify emails and update the tiers.

→ Reporting: bring matched ad exposure, tracked site activity and CRM deals into an account-level view. Compare results by segment. Use what you find to choose the next audience, page or follow-up to improve.

2/ Open rates.

3/ Impressions from people who could never buy.

→ Count the accounts on your list that saw you.

4/ Meetings booked that never turn into pipeline.

→ Search your account list in Clay by the job titles you sell to, and keep each person's name, title and LinkedIn URL.
→ Run them through a waterfall. Prospeo checks first for a verified email and mobile, and whatever it can't find goes to the next provider. Ours is LeadMagic.

6/ Most of the GTM advice you read online.

7/ More SDRs sending more cold email.

→ More volume on a weak list gets you more of the same result. I'd fix the list before I added a seat.
→ Then let content warm the accounts up.
→ Give Claude last month's call transcripts. Ask it to list every question and objection in the buyer's words and count how often each came up. Write a post for each of the top 5.
→ We pull our topics from sales calls, and those posts book us 50+ meetings a month.
→ Each week, export who reacted to or commented on those posts. Anyone at a target account gets enriched in Clay and goes into a sequence that opens on the post they engaged with.

8/ One template sent to 10,000 people.

→ A funding round or a new hire changes what a company needs that month.
→ Clay can watch your account list for both, plus job changes for the champions you already know. Stack them. Once an account has 3 or more signals, email it that week.

9/ Which team gets credit for the lead.

→ Omniscient Digital had 189 leads say an AI tool sent them. HubSpot's first-touch tracking credited 28.
→ Log 2 sources on every deal: what your software tracked first, and what the buyer told you on the first call.
→ That second source is where AI search shows up. Ahrefs studied 75,000 brands, and the ones with more web mentions showed up more in AI answers. Backlinks barely mattered.

If your outbound isn't booking meetings and you've decided the copy is the problem, stop. Rewriting it won't fix anything.

The copy is almost never what's broken. It's one of the 7 steps underneath it, and they only work in one order.

Here's the system I'd rebuild from zero, in the exact sequence I'd build it:

1. Infrastructure
Nobody wants to start here. 20 secondary domains, 40 mailboxes, a two-week warm-up before a single cold send. The primary never sends, because reputation attaches to the domain and it's the one asset you can't replace. This caps your volume at ~1,000 sends a day. Write that number down. It sizes every decision that follows.

2. Data
Almost everyone lives in three sources: LinkedIn, ZoomInfo, Apollo.
Same filters + list every competitor is emailing this week. I mapped 60+. The base I'd run is 6 providers, because each one is strong exactly where another is thin. I'd rather email 400 rows that each have a reason than 4,000 that don't. The reason is what you open with.

3. Enrichment
One provider always reports a coverage number that looks fine. What it can't tell you is who it never had a shot at. A real run inside Claude Code: Apollo returned 153 contacts, a second pass ended at 149 verified. Four were invisible on one provider alone. Order the waterfall cheapest-first, and only pay the expensive one for the rows the cheap ones missed.

4. Scoring
This step exists to make the list smaller. Tier three gets nothing. No sequence, no touches, no capacity. Every send into a bad-fit account is one that never reached a good one, and you only have 1,000.

5. Signals
Fit just narrows the list. A signal is the thing that tells you to send this week instead of next quarter. A company posting three SDR roles just told you its pipeline problem in public. If you can't write the first line of the email straight off the signal, it isn't a signal yet.

6. Copy
Only now does anything get written. I ran reply data across 11K campaigns and 132K snapshots. Three frameworks keep coming back: open with their number, reference the hire, name the mutual connection. One variable per variant, or the result tells you nothing you can use.

7. Send and measure
Four touches, and the fourth is the last. Campaign level only says the campaign worked. Break it to the framework and you find out what to actually write next Tuesday.

Find your broken step:

landing in spam, copy unchanged = step 1
same list your competitors email = step 2
coverage looks fine, reach is thin = step 3
reply rate low on good copy = step 4, you're emailing the wrong accounts
can't write a true first line = step 5
great targeting, weak replies = step 6
something worked, nobody knows what = step 7

Every step caps the next one. Fix the earliest broken one first.

If it all feels random, you're starting at step 6. Go back to step 1.

Our team puts out 200+ LinkedIn posts a month across 150,000+ followers.

So I put together a cheatsheet on how to build pipeline with LinkedIn.

 1. Your Profile

Every section has one job.

 >Picture: 80% face, clean background
 > Headline: "I help X do Y." Mobile crops it around 40 characters
 >Banner: social proof + one clear offer.
 > About: hook, then proof, then the problem you solve, then a CTA.
 >Featured: one gated resource that captures the email, for great value

2. Anatomy of a Post

Every post that works has 4 parts:

 → Hook (stops the scroll)
 → Re-hook (earns the "see more" click)
 → Value (the reason they stay)
 → CTA (the reason they act)

Frameworks I lean on when I'm stuck: PAS (Problem, Agitate, Solution), AIDA (Attention, Interest, Desire, Action), BAB (Before, After, Bridge).

3. Hooks

Keep them 40 to 70 characters. One idea with a curiosity gap.

My best-performing hooks do one of two things:

 → Lead with a number ("These are the 6 AI agents we deploy across our         >$10M ARR clients")
 → Lead with an authority anchor ("Across 100 outreach sequences, these 4 signals won")

Numbers are usually the winning formula for us.

 4. Your Content system

They say best practices are to post across a funnel:

 → 50% reach (broad, relatable, top of funnel)
 → 25% authority (frameworks, breakdowns, proof)
 → 25% convert (offers, lead magnets, case studies)

I find this still works.  Two other core concepts:

→ Design is 80% of the post.
→ Post 3 to 5 times a week. Consistency compounds.

5. The Best Part

This is where 99% of "LinkedIn advice" stops.  3 plays we run every single week:

 → Your engagers: capture everyone who reacts and comments on your posts, enrich them, then retarget. They already raised their hand.

 → Competitor engagers: capture who's engaging with your competitors' content. They are potentially shopping your category.

 → Social listening: find people literally asking for what you sell ("anyone know a good X?") and reach out while the intent is actually hot. Surprisingly you might be able to find 2-3 of these per month. But you have a much higher likelihood of closing them.

I run outbound for 15 clients from one terminal, 23M+ emails and counting. My most-used lever is the delete key.

Every vendor in this space sells you more. More inboxes + enrichment + touches, a bigger list. That advice made sense when inboxes were open and domains were cheap to burn.

The clients of mine who broke their revenue ceiling did the opposite. They cut the motion down. Here are the 5 things I delete first, in order.

1. The list

A one-filter list is a phone book with a logo on it. Before a single send I score every account on four dimensions:

- funding
- firmographics
- tech stack
- growth signals.

Score the whole list on fit and timing, and send to the top slice only.

2. The redundant tool.

Most stacks run the same job through two tools, and one is failing without ever throwing an error. A tool should keep its slot only if it answers in seconds, errors loudly, and returns clean data.

Collapse the rest into one waterfall: Wiza, then FullEnrich across 20+ providers, then Prospeo for the gaps.

List every tool and the one job it owns.

3. The volume per inbox.

Sending harder from the same inboxes is how domains die. When a domain's reputation collapses, it takes every queued email with it. The fix is lower volume spread across more warmed inboxes.

The inbox policy I run:
- Warm-up: two weeks before a single cold send.
- Auth: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC on day one.
- Cap: 20 to 25 sends per inbox per day.
- Complaints: under 0.1%, one or two per thousand, or the domain is done.

It is boring, and it is why we land 95%+ in the primary inbox. Audit sends per inbox. Any inbox over 25 a day, redistribute the volume or add inboxes.

4. The human doing robot work.

If a model does the task at 90% of your quality in a fraction of the time, it is no longer a human task. Keeping a person on it is a tax you pay every week.

The split is simple:
- Give the model: list building, enrichment, scoring, sequence drafts, pre-call research.
Keep the human: the offer, the targeting call, the one reply that closes a deal.

5. The vanity metric.

I do not care how many meetings you booked. Meetings are the easiest number in outbound to inflate. Pipeline by source is the only board I trust. Tag every opportunity to the campaign or signal that made it, wire RB2B or Vector into the CRM, and kill any source under your bar.

I rescore accounts daily, and 20% of my pipeline comes from ones marked cold. Rebuild your dashboard on pipeline by source. Delete every vanity tile.

One more: kill the ask-first email. "Hop on a 15-minute call?" is why reply rates cratered.

Give something usable before you ask for anything.

Before you add a tool, a channel, or a follow-up, ask what you could delete instead.

If you're doing GTM, you might want to save this...

(these are the insights we gathered from building GTM systems for 275+ companies)

ICP & targeting

1. One ICP. Nail it, then expand. 3 ICPs on day one is 3 half-built campaigns.
2. Define by pain, not job title. A title and a headcount band is a filter.
3. Stack intent signals before you send. Signal-triggered lists reply at 15-25%. Static lists, 3.4%.
4. Build the list in Clay.
5. Job changes are a buying trigger. A champion who moves takes the problem with them.
6. Track tech stack. If they run your competitor, they already believe in the problem. You're selling a switch.
7. Watch hiring. A company posting 3 SDR roles just told you they're investing in outbound.
8. Layer funding on top. Recently raised means budget and a deadline.
9. Score by signal density. A 20-person startup firing 5 signals outranks a Fortune 500 firing none.
10. Re-cut the ICP every quarter. Pull the last 30-50 closed-won domains and rebuild the filters from those.

Outbound setup

11. Never cold email from your primary domain. Buy separate ones.
12. Buy 15-20 sending domains and 40 mailboxes, each on its own IP. Cap it at 2-3 mailboxes per domain and split them 50/50 across Google Workspace and Microsoft 365.
13. Warm for 2 weeks minimum. Don't send a prospect anything from a new domain for its first 14 days live.
14. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC on day one. p=none is enough to clear Google, Yahoo, and Outlook. Skip it and you're in spam before the first send.
15. Scale by mailbox count. 20-25 sends a day per mailbox is the ceiling, so spread it across 40 inboxes instead of overloading a few.
16. Pick one sending tool and stay. Switching mid-campaign resets your reputation.
17. Verify EVERY address before it goes out. Under 2% bounce is the safe zone. Above it you're burning the domain.
18. Check domain health weekly in Postmaster v2. It's a pass or a needs-work, nothing in between.
19. Split inbound and outbound infrastructure. Different tools, different domains, different rules.
20. Keep backup domains warming in the background. Domains have a shelf life, replace them every 9-12 months.

Cold email

21. Relevance beats personalization. One accurate line on why you're writing proves you did the homework.
22. 3 words get the subject opened. The body sells.
23. Under 80 words.
24. One CTA. "Worth a conversation?" is enough.
25. Lead with their problem. "Struggling with X" beats "We do Y".
26. Plan 4-7 touches, then stop. 58% of replies still land on step one.
27. A/B test the offer. "Free audit" against "strategy call" is a word tweak. Change what you're actually offering.
28. Write like a human. Human-edited emails reply at 5.1%, pure AI at 2.4%. The edit is the whole difference.
29. Fix the list before you touch send time. "Best time to send" is what people optimize when the list is bad.
30. Replies are the metric. Opens are unreliable and replies are pipeline.

LinkedIn content

31. Post from the founder. Company page organic reach fell 66% in 2 years.
32. Post 3-5x a week. More frequency still lifts reach. There's no penalty in the data.
33. Narrate the work. Real numbers, real workflows, real outcomes. Manufactured takes get scrolled.
34. Your hook has under 3 seconds. Put the number in the first line.
35. Gate lead magnets by hand. LinkedIn now limits comments made by automation.
36. Documents out-reach everything. Docs 1.39x, video 0.86x and falling.
37. Repurpose everything.
38. Engage 15 minutes before and after you post. The first hour decides distribution.
39. Content is top of funnel for outbound. Prospects who've seen your posts reply at 3x the rate.
40. Specificity beats polish. "47 meetings from one workflow" is the whole post. A vague promise about your pipeline is nothing.

LinkedIn ads

41. Ads buy familiarity. Warm them up before the cold email hits.
42. Upload your target account list.
43. Retarget website visitors. The pricing-page visit is a signal. Put the ad in front of them before the email goes out.
44. Ads from a person's profile pull about 2x the CTR of company ads. No lead gen forms on them, so no direct conversions either.
45. $10 a day is the floor. $3-5K a month is the reality.
46. Make the ad look like your organic posts. Anything that reads as an ad gets scrolled.
47. Chase penetration over frequency. Past 8 exposures, click probability starts falling.
48. Promote your best organic posts.
49. Lead gen forms for bottom of funnel only. Leads expire after 90 days now, so sync them to CRM the same day.
50. Measure influenced pipeline. Revenue attribution reports at company level now. Use it.

The flywheel

51. Outbound alone is a treadmill. The list gets worked once, then next month starts from zero.
52. Content is air cover for outbound. 68% of buyers have a front-runner before they start looking.
53. Ads build familiarity before the email lands. 5 impressions in, a cold email feels warm.
54. Outbound generates your content. Every objection, win, and lost deal is a post.
55. Point all 3 channels at the same account list. Same rows, same week, or nothing compounds.
56. Build in the order above: list, domains, email, content, ads. One layer at a time.
57. The flywheel compounds monthly. Month 1 is a list and 3 posts. Month 6 is replies from people who saw the posts.
58. Warm outbound is where this is going. Pull the post engagers into Clay and sequence them first.
59. Content engagers are your best targets. 3 post likes beat any third-party intent signal.
60. Every channel feeds the others. The post builds the ad audience, the ad drives the site visit, and outbound closes.

AI in GTM

61. AI replaces tasks, not judgment. Vercel's lead agent took over inbound qualification and 9 SDRs moved to outbound.
62. AI writes bad outbound by default. Give it your voice, your ICP, and your real signals or it writes for nobody.
63. Clay plus AI is an unfair advantage. Enrichment and signal scoring at a scale no SDR team matches.
64. Build AI workflows before you buy AI tools. An n8n flow built once runs on every client after that. A rented tool bills you again for every seat.
65. AI SDRs work best as augmentation. 11x's own CEO: "I don't think AI SDRs work."
66. Use LLMs to score and prioritize signals. Ours runs every account through a classification prompt with closed-won plus signal data as the rubric. 110 companies tiered in under a minute.
67. Automate the first mile. Keep the last mile human. Claude pulls and scores the list. The Tier 1 message still goes out by hand.
68. Let AI do 70% of the draft. You own the last 30%, and that's the part that ships.
69. Connect the stack with MCP. I run 18 of these daily in Claude Code: Clay, Apollo, Instantly, Attio, Supabase.
70. Small teams are pulling ahead, slowly. Revenue per employee moved 9-17%.

Tech stack

71. CRM is the foundation. Pick one and commit. Watch the bill. Everyone is repricing to credits.
72. Clay for enrichment and signal stacking.
73. Apollo for prospecting data on a budget. Best value per valid email. Database size is the wrong number to shop on.
74. Layer enrichment tools. Cheapest and cleanest first, escalate only on a miss. With a full waterfall (Wiza, FullEnrich, Prospeo) coverage can push past 90%.
75. One sequencing tool. Instantly for volume, lemlist when the sequence spans channels.
76. Split your LinkedIn tool from your email tool. One suspension shouldn't take both channels down.
77. Taplio for scheduling. Never for auto-commenting.
78. Check your tools are still alive. Common Room went to Zoom, Salesloft merged into Clari. Your stack diagram is probably out of date.
79. PredictLeads for company-level intent. Hiring, funding, and tech changes before your CRM sees them.
80. Fix the process before the stack. $50K of tools with no ICP is expensive noise.

Metrics & attribution

81. Revenue closed is the only real metric. Everything else is a leading indicator.
82. Stop celebrating meetings booked. 50 meetings and 0 closed deals is a loss.
83. Track cost per opportunity. A lead is a form fill. An opportunity has a buyer with budget attached.
84. Measure reply rate, not open rate. Apple Mail Privacy killed open tracking for good.
85. Attribution is multi-touch. That deal touched content, ads, and outbound.
86. Ask "how did you hear about us?" on every form. Software misses 81% of the buying journey.
87. Build a weekly GTM scorecard. 10 numbers, each with the value that means you already have a problem.
88. Set a coverage ratio and hold it.
89. Measure channel contribution monthly.
90. AI traffic is breaking your dashboards. Roughly 70% of it lands in GA4 as "Direct".

Mistakes that kill pipeline

91. More volume is never the answer. Campaigns under 50 recipients reply at 5.8%. Big blasts, 2.1%.
92. Blasting 10K emails a day. It kills the domain and the brand with it.
93. Skipping deliverability setup. Outlook now hard-rejects with 550 5.7.515 and you find out after the campaign has gone out.
94. Hiring SDRs, human or AI, before there's a system. Nothing fixes a broken offer except fixing the offer.
95. Automating LinkedIn comments and DMs. LinkedIn is banning the tools themselves now.
96. Building on scraped LinkedIn data. Proxycurl is dead. LinkedIn is suing the rest.
97. Treating outbound as a silo. Disconnected from content and ads is money left on the table.
98. Optimizing copy when targeting is the problem. Better words will never fix the wrong audience.
99. Being invisible to AI assistants. 51% of buyers now start their research in a chatbot.
100. Chasing AI shortcuts over fundamentals. An agent can push a campaign into Instantly in minutes. If the domains never warmed and the list was never scored, it just lands in spam faster.

A scoring script you write once, so the same account scores the same on every run. Firmographics first, because the cheapest filter should run before you spend a credit.

3. Find the people
Prospeo io and Clay, starting from the domain and building the list live. Pull the whole buying committee: the champion, the decision maker, and whoever gets blamed if it fails.

4. Verify the contact
Work email and mobile in the same pass. Cheapest provider first, and waterfall for the emails the first provider doesn't find.

5. Write from your frameworks
Claude drafts from the angles that already converted, because the folder holds them with the numbers attached.

6. Preflight the send
SPF, DKIM and DMARC set-up on every sending domain, volume spread across mailboxes, and any contact already part of another sequence is removed. Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook all enforce this on bulk senders now.

7. Launch and learn
Instantly for volume email, Lemlist for calls and multichannel. Replies and booked meetings go back to the CRM, and what converted goes back into the folder so your workflow can learn by itself.

Claude Code scored and tiered 110 companies in under a minute when @itsivanfalco and I built a campaign live.

Every time I reviewed a list, I'd delete accounts, fix openers, and move on. The next run made the same mistakes, because I never wrote down why.

So this is the order I set it up in every folder before a campaign goes live:

1. Start a corrections log. Every account I remove from a list gets 1 line on why. That log becomes the first draft of the ICP file.

2. Split icp md into 4 parts: eligibility, exclusions, priority and unknowns. A hiring signal can raise priority, but I still remove any account that hits an exclusion.

3. Give every account a status with the reason next to it: exclude, hold, suppress or proceed. Without the reason, Claude picks skipped accounts back up as fresh leads on the next run.

4. Build an approved-claims md with the source, segment, date and exact wording for every proof point. Claude can only use a result that's in that file.

5. Split "send to Instantly" into 4 actions:

- export the list
- create a draft campaign
- upload contacts
- activate.

Claude can do the first 3. Activate needs my approval, and I block it in the tool permissions, because a line in CLAUDE md won't stop a send.

6. Test on 5 accounts where I already know the answer: one that fits, an excluded business model, one with missing data, a current customer and a stale signal. I write the expected status before the run. If Claude gets one wrong, I fix the file and rerun that exact case.

If I make the same correction twice, I edited an email and never touched the file.

We’ve built outbound systems for 275+ companies at @Frontal_AI. If I were setting one up from scratch tomorrow, this is everything I’d do, step by step:

New domains need 2 weeks of warm-up before their emails stop landing in spam. Buy them before you pull a single contact, and build the rest of the system while they warm.

Day 1
→ Buy 15 to 20 sending domains and 40 mailboxes, and start the warm-up.
→ Switch on 7 triggers to start. A trigger is a recent change that gives you a reason to email, like a funding round. Give each one an age limit, so a company doesn't rank higher for a round it raised 4 months ago.
→ Work out how many emails you can send a day. Size every list after this to that 1 number.

Week 1
→ Pull your last 30 to 50 customers from the CRM, and use CompanyEnrich to find 50 similar companies for each one.
→ Go through those by hand and cut the bad matches. Search for roofers and you'll get roofing supply shops too.
→ Have Claude sort every company into 3 tiers, best fit first. If it isn't sure about one, it goes down a tier.
→ Write down why every removed company was removed. Without the reason, Claude adds them back on the next run.

Week 2
→ Write 1 first line per trigger, before you have a single name to send it to. Nobody wants to hear "saw you raised a round", so say what the change means for them in that same line.
→ Run the whole setup on 5 companies where you already know the right answer. Make 1 of them a current customer. It should never get an email.

Last days of warm-up
→ Pull the 3 people you want at each company and verify every address that same day. Above a 2% bounce rate, you're burning the domains you just spent 2 weeks warming.

Day 15
→ The first campaign goes out, best-fit companies first.

After launch
→ Re-score every company every day. In Q2, 20% of our pipeline came from companies our CRM had marked cold 30 days earlier.
→ Start from the 3 email frameworks in the article until you've sent 10,000+ emails. After that, write from your own winners.

You won't know which triggers matter most for your product until you have a few months of reply data.

If you're looking to turn buying signals into pipeline, set up these 5 plays in your CRM and do exactly what I describe below:

(these come from building outbound systems for 275+ companies at @Frontal_AI)

1. Reach new leaders in their first 90 days
→ Only act on VP and above, in sales, marketing or revops, under 90 days in the seat.
→ Best-fit accounts get a personal email and a call from a rep. Good fits get an automated sequence: congrats, what the last person in the seat did, a direct ask.

2. Reopen the deals you lost when something changes
→ Set the wait by why you lost. Timing: next quarter. Budget: next budget cycle. Competitor: ahead of their renewal. Missing feature: when it ships.
→ When the wait is up, check what changed. If nothing did, the deal goes back to waiting. If something did, the rep who ran the deal messages the contact who pushed for you last time, names the change, and ties it back to why you lost.

3. Reach funded companies in their first week
→ Every Friday, pull rounds from the last 7 days and skip seed.
→ Day 1: the budget owner and the person who'd do the work each get an email about what they'll hire for next.

I was once in this EXACT position. The urge to raise was tied to 3 things that had nothing to do with strategy:

1. Scarcity mindset

If you've never lived in a home where your ceiling is someone else's floor, this part might not land. But for me, raising was about making sure I never had to go back.

Money in the bank meant safety. Safety meant if HeyReach blew up, I could build something else. If that blew up, I could build something after that. I was buying myself permission to keep trying.

I used to tell myself "I cannot NOT make this happen. I'm not going back there." I meant it. I still mean it. But I was treating a fundraise like an emergency exit when what I actually needed was to trust the thing I was already building.

2. I wasn't honest with myself about what I actually wanted to build

I wanted to compete with Clay or Apollo and build the biggest sales engagement platform in the world.

> I said it on calls
> I said it in pitch decks
> I said it to my team

At some point I started believing it.

But deep down I knew it wasn't true. I didn't wake up excited about becoming a multi product beast. I woke up excited about making HeyReach the best LinkedIn outreach tool anyone had ever used.

The problem was, "build the biggest" sounds like ambition. "Build the best version of one thing" sounds small. When you are chasing the VC's "idea of success", building a "non-billion dollar business and being independent" sounds small. But actually it's not - it's the key to freedom, and a true success.

I was repeating someone else's definition of success back to them and calling it my goal. 

3. The startup rat race

The whole VC industry pushes you to be a workaholic. Sleep-deprive yourself. Grind 12 hours a day. 

I was watching 20-something-year-olds in San Francisco who raised millions live like this:

> Windowless bedrooms
> Mattresses on the floor
> 12 hour workdays
> 10 years of grinding to build something that might get disrupted anyway

That's not the life I wanted.

Raising is a tool. It's not an accomplishment. If you can't use the tool well, it's cheaper to not use it at all.

It depends entirely on what kind of business you want to build and what kind of life you want to live while you build it.

text: It took me three years to realize that you’re almost always better off bootstrapping your company than raising money.

You can just:

- Start an account on X
- Share your wins, your failures, and the lessons 
- Engage with everyone in your space 3-4x a day
- Connect with the creators and founders worth knowing
- Get your whole team posting alongside you

And slowly, you build a content loop where you're everywhere.

It was the best decision I made when I was just starting. 

My only regret is not starting sooner.

I remember the moment we hit $400K ARR.

Our investors from my previous company said: 

“Nice, from here everything is upside.” 

But before that, it was really hazy, just a loop of trying to do this and that.

> Hundred times of quitting
> Nobody believing
> Investors saying ‘no’ anytime we mentioned our product

We'd been stuck between $8-9K MRR for like six months, and we couldn't scale past it. 

That was the moment we decided we needed to niche down, so we niched down to lead gen agencies, and that's when we doubled. We hit $19K, then the next month we doubled again, hit $30K-something, then doubled and doubled.

It was proof that we had potential product market fit, and our ICP was lead-gen agencies. 

The product was good for a given ICP, so we doubled down on that. 

> We iterated 
> We listened to the feedback 
> And we were super focused on that segment

Lesson there.

We hit $10M ARR on pure word-of-mouth. 100% organic, 2,600+ free trials a month, basically $0 on ads. If I had a chance to do it all over again, I wouldn’t do it this way for sure.

Because word-of-mouth is an effect. You can earn it, you can engineer the conditions for it. What you can't do is open a dashboard and turn it up when you need $200K more in pipeline this quarter. It speeds up when it feels like it, and slows down when it feels like it. You're always slightly at its mercy.

The moment this realization dawned upon me was mid-2025. After months of adding $1M a month, our MRR stagnated for three weeks straight.

We just... stopped. I panicked hard. I thought this was it, we'd hit the ceiling, the "stuck" stage @RetentionAdam talks about.

And I had no lever to pull. There was no campaign to launch or budget to push, nothing I could turn on to fix it. All I could do was wait and pray it was seasonality.

It was. Growth came back.

But those three weeks taught me something I couldn't unlearn: if your growth can stall for no reason you can see, then recover just as quietly, you don't really control it. You're a passenger.

That's the trap with organic. It feels amazing, so you lean into it and tell yourself you've cracked growth. You haven't. You've been carried by something you can't steer, and one day it slows down and you have no idea why or how to start it again.

We'd even tried ads for a month early on and killed them, because organic kept outpacing them. So we leaned in harder, and got a little addicted to growth we didn't have to pay for.

Then at $10M, I finally built the channels we'd avoided for years.
@VukConfidential and Ilija from our team started cracking ads for real.

First month: $800 spent, 17 customers, 3x ROI. Small, but the difference was everything. It was growth I could turn up on purpose.

Word-of-mouth hadn't stopped working. It still is a very big growth driver for us. It’s just that I never wanted to feel that helpless about my own company again.

Earn word-of-mouth with product and positioning. But never mistake it for a strategy that you can always depend on.

I've been "the CEO" of @heyreach_io for 3 years now. And the job I do today has almost nothing in common with the job I was doing in year one.

I started thinking about this after a tense weekly meeting a while back, when Leon Spremo asked me in front of the whole team:

"What do you actually do in this company?! We code the tool, Ilija sells it... what's your job here?"

I didn't have a good answer back then. Now, on the other side of $10M ARR, fully bootstrapped, I think I finally do:

"CEO" is a different job at every stage. The title stays the same, the work gets completely rewritten every time you add a zero.

Here's the map.

1/ $0 - $1M

You are just a product guy with a fancy title.

No real titles, no real departments besides "product" and "growth". Your only goal is to build something that solves a real problem and find PMF. The company is in dying mode until you do, and your whole job is to not let it die.

We launched @heyreach_io months away from bankruptcy and then got stuck at $8-9K MRR until October. Nothing about that period felt like being a "CEO". I was gathering feedback, wireframing, shipping, fixing, begging people to try the tool.

If your calendar is full of "strategy" meetings at this stage, you are roleplaying a CEO instead of saving your company.

2/ $1M - $10M

Now you (probably) have PMF, and the job flips: you stop being "the best" at product/marketing/sales in your own company, and you replicate yourself.

3 areas:

a) Set the direction. Not "because YOU are the CEO and you think that's the way to go". Quite the opposite... you canalize the inputs from your heads, your gut, and the market into an educated guess. Someone has to take the single responsibility for fail or success. That's you.

b) Hire the best heads. The people who can take you to $10M won't apply to your job ad, you can't pay them what they're truly worth, and a $100M company already tried to poach them a dozen times. Selling them on your business is 10x harder than fundraising (even tho we never managed to fundraise lol).

c) Enable them. Resources, mentors, untied hands, full ownership. Jump in to solve stuff WITH them when it's burning.

Ilija joined our previous company as employee #5, not speaking English, doing his emails through Google Translate. Today he's @heyreach_io's CRO and earns more than me and Stefan (my co-founder) combined.

That's what replicating yourself looks like. They become better than you, and you celebrate it.

3/ $10M+

Honestly, I'm still figuring this one out.

When I first wrote this framework we were at $4M, and my whole answer for this phase was "I don't know (yet)".

We crossed $10M+ in 29 months. 6 months into this phase, here's what I see so far:

- hire seniors who've already done it, and remove yourself from operations completely
- pick your top 3 battles, consciously drop the rest (Vuk taught me this one)
- expand the TAM every year (new features, audiences, products), or you failed at your job
- stay operational in exactly ONE thing

For me, that one thing is product. I gather the feedback, simplify it, wireframe the feature. Everything after that is reviewing others' work.

But one belief survived every stage:

The CEO should be the CPO.

The best lead list on LinkedIn is free. It's the ~100 people who reacted to your last 5 posts. Takes 30 minutes to pull.

Here's how I'd build it 👇

1. Start with your 5 most on-topic posts, not your best-performing ones.

A viral post pulls reactors from way outside your ICP. A post that spoke straight to your buyer pulls ~20 of exactly the right people. 5 of those and you're at ~100 warm leads.

2. Pull your repeat reactors to the top.

Someone who reacted to 3 of your posts is in a different league from someone who reacted once. Intent stacks. Intersect your reactor lists and surface the repeat engagers first. That overlap is the closest thing to a free buying signal LinkedIn gives you.

3. Clean it hard, because reactors import raw.

There's no job-title filter on import. Every reaction lands in your list as a lead: competitors watching you, job seekers, peers being nice, people who caught the post through a repost and will never buy.

LinkedIn caps you at ~100 connection requests a week. That cap turns your list into a budget, and every off-ICP reactor you leave in spends one of those requests on someone who was never going to buy.

Run two filters before you send: job title and company fit.

4. Suppress anyone you've already touched.

Existing clients. Anyone sitting in another campaign. Hitting the same person from two directions is how you look disorganized and burn a warm lead for good. Exclude them once, globally.

5. Never send a connection request to someone you're already connected to.

Split the list by connection status. The ones already in your network get a direct message. The rest get a request. Sending "let's connect" to a 1st-degree connection is the fastest way to look like a bot.

6. Open with the exact post they reacted to.

"You reacted to my post on X" beats "I saw you're into GTM" every single time. That one detail is what turns a reply into a real conversation, and it's the only place your copy actually earns its keep.

30 minutes, start to finish. No scraping or cold data to buy.

Just the people already paying attention to you, sorted by how warm they actually are.

Reply rate is the most misleading number in outbound.

I looked at 96,000 campaigns on HeyReach. For most teams, reply rate was the wrong thing to watch the entire time.

The number to track instead 👇

Reply rate blends two separate problems into one score:
→ did people accept your request? (a targeting question)
→ did they reply after you messaged? (a messaging question)

When it drops, you can't tell which one broke. So you rewrite your copy when the real problem was your list. Or you rip apart your targeting when the opener was the issue.

The number that actually isolates it:

RTA: Replies ÷ accepted connections.

It measures your messaging alone, and the benchmarks from those 96k campaigns are clean:
→ under 10%: something's broken, stop and fix it
→ around 18%: median, you're average
→ 28% and up: top tier

One stat that stuck with me: 10.7% of those campaigns had accepted connections and still got zero replies. People said yes, and nothing that followed earned a single response.

Average and elite teams send the same volume. The elite ones just say something specific to a tighter list.

An accept and a reply are two different decisions. People accept at almost zero effort. They only reply when it's relevant. Don’t track the both as a single number.

Sending accounts get restricted for behavior against a limit. LinkedIn caps you at around 200 actions a day, and almost everything counts, a profile view, a like, a message.

In the last 12 months, our customers ran nearly 100,000 LinkedIn outreach campaigns through @heyreach_io.

Our team studied acceptance rates, replies, sender setups, campaign size and duration across the whole dataset.

We put everything we found into one report: what good performance looks like, where campaigns break and what to fix before scaling.

Here are 50 LinkedIn outreach rules from the data that can help you build more pipeline:

First, know what “good” actually looks like.

1. Use the median as your primary benchmark. The averages were higher across all three core metrics, so the median gives you a more realistic picture of a typical campaign.

2. A typical campaign had 20.75% of its connection requests accepted, while the average across the full dataset was 23.85%.

3. An acceptance rate below 12.97% was weak. Once it moved above 31.78%, the campaign entered the stronger-performing range.

4. The report’s reply-rate benchmark was 22.22% at the median and 25.19% on average.

5. On that reported reply-rate metric, anything below 13.37% was weak, while anything above 33.33% was strong.

6. Reply-to-acceptance rate, or RTA, had an 18.10% median and a 21.23% average.

7. RTA fell into weak territory below 9.62% and strong territory above 28.89%.

8. RTA is calculated by dividing replies by accepted connections. It isolates what happened after someone agreed to connect and keeps the earlier stages of the funnel separate.

9. Put differently, a typical batch of 100 connection requests produced about 21 acceptances and fewer than four replies.

10. In 10.7% of campaigns, people accepted the connection request and then nobody replied. Not one person.

11. Another 15% of campaigns converted fewer than one in every ten accepted connections into a reply.

12. Combined, roughly one in four campaigns with accepted connections still produced almost no real conversations. Acceptance alone can make these campaigns look healthier than they are.

Use the numbers to diagnose the right problem.

13. When acceptance is weak, start upstream. The likely problem is the ICP, the quality of the list, the sender profile or the connection request itself.

14. When acceptance is healthy but RTA is weak, the list has already done its job. The first message or the sequence is now the more likely problem.

15. Treat overall reply rate as an outcome metric. It cannot diagnose the leak by itself, and any comparison is meaningless until you confirm which denominator is being used.

16. When RTA stays low across every campaign, the opening message is usually the common failure point.

17. When RTA changes significantly from one campaign to another, the message probably fits some segments but not others. That points to an ICP-to-message mismatch.

18. Do not rebuild the whole sequence first. Validate the opener, then check whether each follow-up gives the prospect a new reason to reply.

19. If acceptance suddenly falls, check suppression hygiene first, then the number of pending invitations, and finally the sending pace.

20. If acceptance remains healthy while replies decline, test the first two sentences of the message and the timing between steps before changing everything else.

21. A high total reply rate with very few positive replies can still be a bad result. It usually means the targeting or the relevance is generating objections instead of pipeline.

22. If replies arrive during steps one and two but disappear afterward, the next follow-up probably adds no new angle, proof or useful information.

23. If replies stay low across every step, stop polishing the sequence. Pause the campaign and rebuild a smaller, tighter list.

24. Track how quickly your team answers an interested reply. If that response time is high, adjust staffing windows so someone is available when the segment tends to answer.

Test without creating more noise.

25. Run Step 1 variations against the same audience, with the same timing, and change only one element. Otherwise you will never know what caused the result.

26. Do not judge a variation before it reaches at least 50 accepted connections. Below that threshold, you are mostly reacting to randomness.

27. Track positive replies separately from total replies. A polite rejection and genuine buying intent should never count as the same outcome.

28. Record the audience, timing, message change and result for every test. If performance improves, you should be able to trace the lift back to one decision.

29. Use one dashboard to compare campaigns and senders, then use another to compare segments. Blending both views makes the source of the problem harder to see.

30. Keep every KPI definition fixed from week to week. A changing denominator can manufacture an improvement that never actually happened.

Build the campaign so it can survive scale.

31. One HeyReach benchmark found that blank connection requests averaged 27% acceptance, compared with 22% for requests containing text.

32. Test both within your own audience: a blank request versus a short note that gives one specific, timely reason to connect.

33. If you use a connection note, give the prospect one current reason to connect. Do not turn the note into a product pitch or add a link.

34. Personalization matters most after the connection is accepted. Targeting and sender credibility do more of the work before that point.

35. The guide caps personalization at two meaningful inputs per contact. Adding more signals created more work without improving conversion.

36. Store the reason for the outreach and the source that proves it. Fields such as trigger_reason and proof_link make every personalized opener auditable.

37. Map one or two adjacent stakeholders inside each target account before launching. If the primary contact is wrong, you already know who else may own the problem.

38. Give every follow-up a different job. One should reconnect to the original context, one should offer something concrete, and the final one should close the loop cleanly.

39. Use one suppression list across every sender. Without it, two people from your team can contact the same prospect and destroy the trust you were trying to build.

40. Apply global stop rules for replies, booked meetings and do-not-contact requests. Once a prospect acts, every sender should stop automatically.

Finally, scale the part that is already working.

41. Campaigns with fewer than 100 contacts averaged 21.43% acceptance.

42. Campaigns with more than 1,000 contacts averaged 19.35% acceptance. That is a decline of only 2.08 percentage points from the smallest campaigns.

43. The reported reply-rate metric stayed between 21.67% and 23.08% across the different volume tiers. Volume alone is a poor explanation for falling replies.

44. When a large campaign underperforms, inspect the list before rewriting the copy. Scale usually exposes weak segmentation and lower-fit prospects before it exposes a writing problem.

45. Single-sender campaigns had a 22.22% median reported reply rate. Campaigns using six to 20 senders performed better, reaching 25%.

46. Once campaigns used 50 or more senders, the median reported reply rate fell to 20.33%. More sender accounts were not associated with better reply performance.

47. Campaigns running for fewer than 30 days showed a 13.33% median acceptance rate and a 14.29% reported reply rate.

48. Campaigns running for 180 days or more showed 26.99% acceptance and a 28.26% reported reply rate.

49. Do not read the duration numbers as proof that keeping a weak campaign alive will improve it. Part of the gap is survivorship: campaigns that work stay live, while weak ones get paused or rebuilt.

50. The order (that matters): fix targeting until people accept, fix the post-acceptance message until they reply, and only then add more volume.

How we bootstrapped HeyReach to $17M+ ARR in 3 years:

$139/mo → $1M ARR
AppSumo bought us time.
We focused on lead-gen agencies.
Unlimited LinkedIn senders for one fixed price.

$1M → $2M ARR
Built the API, webhooks and integrations with Clay, Instantly and Smartlead.
Agencies could add LinkedIn outreach to the workflows they already used.

$2M → $3M ARR

$3M → $6M ARR
Added quarterly and annual plans.
Ran LinkedIn outreach events with Clay across Europe.
Cut ads after two months of testing. Growth sped up.

$6M → $7M ARR
Shipped workspaces and user permissions.
Agencies could separate client accounts and control who had access.
Missing those features had been our biggest reason for lost deals and churn.

$7M → $8M ARR
Launched our creator program and LinkedIn MCP.
Creators taught the workflows. Customers could run outreach through AI agents.
Reached 2,600+ trials a month without ad spend.

$8M → $10M ARR
Gave creators higher commissions and sent them leads for their agencies.
Affiliate links accounted for $1M ARR.
We contacted old trial users who had started visiting our website again.
An $800 ad test brought in 17 customers.

$10M → $16M ARR
@Vick_Mucunski rebuilt onboarding and flagged customers who stopped using the product.
Revenue churn fell from 9% to 7%.
Recovered 30% of failed-payment revenue in four days.
Helped customers use more seats and new workflows. Some cancellation calls became upgrades.

$16M → $17M+ ARR
188 existing customers paid us another $100,865 in 30 days.
The offer: pay for 3 months, get 6.
Discounts on quarterly and annual plans when paid upfront.

What I've added above are some of the major growth plays and decisions at each milestone. Full breakdown below.

Building a SaaS in 2026?

Here's my best advice after we went from almost bankrupt to $17M ARR, fully bootstrapped:

1. Don't invent a category. We launched into a market with 400+ tools.

2. Ship early. We called our multi-sender feature “multi-account outreach” until customers renamed it for us.

3. Pick one ICP. Building for everyone kept us stuck.

4. Get profitable first. Then immediately obsess over PMF.

5. If you're not growing, you're dying.

6. At the start, CEO is a fancy title. You're product, sales, marketing, ops and support. That's why I believe the CEO should also be the CPO.

7. Keep the team as small as possible.

8. Great customer support is the real growth hack. At our worst, we had 200+ tickets a day and 10-hour first responses.

9. Be patient. You probably won't achieve much in the first 3-6 months. That's normal.

Venture was already an unnatural way to build most businesses. AI just makes it more obvious imo.

We're getting tools to build with fewer people and less money... and somehow the thing we're supposed to celebrate is raising a round so big you HAVE to build a huge company.

We bootstrapped @heyreach_io to $17M ARR. If we hire people we can't afford, I can't pay their salaries with a story about where we'll be in 3 years. The business has to pay them.

That's the part of the VC game that bothers me. You can keep buying customers who'll never pay back what they cost, show everyone a growing revenue chart and raise again. More money comes in, more people join, everyone thinks it's working.

Then the next round doesn't happen and suddenly "it didn't work out."

The people who took a pay cut for your equity probably have a longer version of that story.

AI should reduce how much of your company you need to sell to get it built. I don't see why it should buy founders another few years of pretending the numbers will fix themselves.

Cold email has been dying for years already.

It just won't be a sudden snap where everyone wakes up and it's gone. It gets a little more annoying, a little more expensive and a lot more laborious every year.

A few years ago, you could find a billionaire's email, press send and honestly expect it to reach them.

Today? Good luck.

Before the first cold email even goes out, you need a gazillion things set up. Extra domains, inboxes, warmup, DNS, blacklists, deliverability... then you start sending and hope you don't burn the domain before you understand if the list or the copy works.

LinkedIn is the better place to start today.

You can launch a campaign right away and within a few hours start seeing what is happening. The feedback isn't perfect, but it narrows things down fast.

Low acceptance usually points you back to the list or profile. No replies after acceptance still leaves a few things to inspect: the message, offer, timing, follow-up, or the rest of the sequence.

Every profile also has a face, work history, posts and mutual connections. There is context before the first message.

IMO, email still has a place inside a multichannel motion. I'd start on LinkedIn, use email where it makes sense, and let content and warm intros do some of the work around both.

Cold email will probably keep working for a long time. There will just be fewer and fewer teams willing to do all that work for one channel.
