text:
Building a SaaS and drowning in good ideas?

So do I, and I've stopped trying to fix that. I built a way to work around it instead.

That's basically the CPO job, and I do believe the CEO should be doing it. Here's how:

1. The roadmap starts with boring inputs

Churn reasons. Closed-lost reasons with their revenue potential next to them. Support tickets. Feature requests never go straight on the list, we write down the problem hiding behind them first.

2. We almost never build what was asked for

Customers care about solving their problem as soon as possible. How it fits the rest of the product is my job, not theirs. Campaign Analytics 2.0 took 50+ user interviews and a rework from scratch.

3. Sometimes the answer is an integration

Our own email sequencer was the obvious next feature. I've said no every time. Our customers already ran Instantly, Smartlead and EmailBison, so we integrated with all three. The first one shipped in a few weeks.

4. We don't have a three-year roadmap

We know roughly 80% of what we'll ship this quarter, maybe 50% of the year. Then we pick three battles and drop the rest.

5. Seven phases, and I'm only operational in the first

Idea, wireframe, design, development, testing, launch, revision. I talk to customers, simplify the feedback, draw the first wireframe, then hand it over and review.

6. When my judgment is wrong, I own the consequences

I switched our support tooling in two days to save $3K a month. It cost us at least $15K a month in churn. I unfckd what I fckd up, then got out of the way of the person who rebuilt the department.

In 2023 we were 3 months away from bankruptcy and stuck at $8K MRR. AppSumo bought us runway that summer, and for the rest of the year LinkedIn outreach we ran ourselves brought in 61.4% of our revenue and 523 qualified meetings we sat in.

If I had to build pipeline on LinkedIn from zero tomorrow, here's how I'd do it:

1. I'd fix my profile before I sent a single request

Everyone you reach out to opens your profile before they decide anything, so that page is essentially doing your selling for you. There are tons of resources and pointers on how to setup your profile up. So I'm not going to repeat that.

2. Most of my time would go into the list

Back in 2023 we measured Sales Navigator handing back around 31% dirty data, and idk what it is today but it isn't zero. So I'd pull the list, check the data is real, cut anyone who hasn't posted in three months, and only then start sending.

The best list I know is free anyway. It's the hundred or so people who reacted to your last 5 posts, it takes 30 minutes to pull, and they already know who you are (given you're posting actively on LinkedIN).

After that I'd stop looking at job titles and start looking for a signal that I can act on, so the outreach is timed well.

3. I'd warm them up before asking for anything

Like something they posted in the last 2-3 days, then send the request. "Nick liked your post" hits their notifications while they're still in there, so by the time the request shows up, you're a familiar name to them.

4. The request goes out empty

27% of blank requests get accepted, against 22% for the ones carrying a note. We arrived at this data point after going through nearly 100k LinkedIn campaigns sent through @heyreach_io.

5. I'd treat the first message like a message

Not an email.

I'd write two lines, ask one thing they can answer without thinking about it, and then leave them alone until they reply.

Don't run NPC sequences like a blank request, then "thanks for accepting!", then a wall of text with a calendar link at the bottom. You've received that one this week. It works 0% of the time.

I'd also answer fast. I try to get to anything that comes in within 15 minutes, cuz that's the cheapest thing on this whole list.

6. Track replies on accepted connections. Not just the reply rate.

Reply rate divides by everyone you sent to, so a campaign can look fine and be dead.

The number I'd prefer tracking is replies over accepted connections.

Low acceptance generally indicates a list problem. But if you get connection acceptance, and still no response, then it might have to do with your copy and framing.

7. I'd only scale once the six above actually work

And I'd do it sideways. Every account carries that same ceiling from step 1 above (200 actions/day on LinkedIn), so more volume has to mean more accounts. 6 to 20 sending accounts is where reply rates peak in our data.

What I wouldn't do is add senders to a campaign that's broken somewhere in 1 through 6. That just spends the limits faster on the same outcome.

Especially when more people match your filters. Here’s how to get past that limit and add more matching prospects to your outreach list.

The limit applies to each lead search. Splitting a large search into smaller groups lets you find more people who match your original filters.

1. Keep the buyer profile fixed.

Use the same roles, company criteria and locations that define your target audience. Split the search without loosening those criteria.

For example, if you target sales leaders in the US and UK at companies with 11-200 employees, create these searches:

- US, 11-50 employees.
- US, 51-200 employees.
- UK, 11-50 employees.
- UK, 51-200 employees.

Keep your current-title query identical across all four.

2. Check which searches still exceed 2,500 results.

Split those into smaller groups. Record the filters, result counts and search URLs. If you split by location again, keep track of which areas you’ve covered.

3. Turn the searches into one clean prospect list.

In @heyreach_io, use Leads → Add Leads → Sales Navigator (Leads) to import each search URL.

You can do this cleanup from Claude Code too. Connect our MCP and ask it to prepare one clean prospect list from those imports, excluding leads with prior outreach recorded in your workspace.

4. Check the fit before using the list.

Open a sample from each group. Confirm the current role and company match your original criteria.

One more thing: save each smaller search and turn on alerts for new results.

LinkedIn will notify you when new people match your filters. Review those matches, remove anyone already on your list or previously contacted, and add the relevant prospects to your next campaign.

You can reuse the searches as your audience changes, without rebuilding the filters every time.

$17M ARR in, and I'm convinced every founder needs a no list. The stuff you WON'T build or do, even when it sounds totally reasonable.

If I wrote mine down today, it'd look like this:

1. Blindly following the AI hype. At one point our roadmap had AI hyper-personalization of messages, an AI LinkedIn SDR and AI profile optimization on it... I'm glad we didn't just run with all of it.

2. The all-in-one outbound platform. Data, LinkedIn, email, CRM, everything in one tool. Back in 2024 that looked like a reasonable plan and we never went for it.

3. An email sequencer. We integrated Instantly, Smartlead and EmailBison instead, and the first integration took a few weeks (compare that against developing a feature). 

4. A three-year roadmap (more on that below).

5. More lifetime deals. AppSumo saved us in 2023 when we had 3 months of cash left. Two years later, selling more of them would have been insane.

If you're starting yours from zero, 3 things I'd do:

1. Write down the problem behind a request before anything else

At @heyreach_io feature requests don't go straight on the roadmap. We write down the underlying problem first, sort it by user satisfaction, frequency and revenue impact, and only later look at the cost of development.

Some requests turn out to be huge. Missing workspaces and user permissions had become our biggest reason for lost deals and churn, so we built them. A request that never gets anywhere near that is a good candidate for your no list.

2. Plan in quarters

We know roughly 80% of what we ship in a quarter and maybe 50% of the year, and tbh past that it's just guesses... and I don't want the team stuck defending them.

So we pick 3 battles for the quarter and consciously drop the rest (Vuk taught me this one). That dropped pile is where your no list starts.

3. Put your old wins on it too

This one's the hardest. For us, what worked at one milestone usually turned into a big problem at the next one, and the lifetime deals above are the best example I have.

Most of the biggest problems we fixed at HeyReach were created by something we celebrated around 6 months earlier.

So every time you hit a new stage, take the plays that got you there and ask one question: would we start this today, at the size we are now?

If the answer is no, it goes on the list, even if it saved your company once.

text:
HeyReach was stuck at $8K MRR for 5 months in 2023.

We didn't even know who we were selling to. Recruiters, individuals, sales teams of every size, agencies... basically anyone with a LinkedIn account.

The pricing didn't help either. We launched at $149/mo per LinkedIn sender, way more expensive than anything on the market, for a buggy product with half the features the competitors had. 

Total disaster. 

So we dropped to $79/mo with discounts for 10+ and 50+ senders and thought we cracked it.

Nope. That's the exact pricing that kept us at $8K.

A month before How to Web in Bucharest, Ilija came to me with this:

"Dude, we've had 597 sales calls so far, and the data says we MUST niche down to agencies! This is the way to go!"

It sounded scary and I was pretty sure recruiters were our vertical (our booth poster at How to Web literally said "next-gen outreach tool for leadgen & recruitment agencies", lol).

The people we met and the energy at that conference are what finally made us push toward agencies. First thing I did when we came back was give the green light to redesign the website and the pricing page, and niche down specifically to lead-gen agencies.

We rebuilt the offer around agencies: unlimited LinkedIn senders for one fixed price.

The next month we 2.5x-ed revenue and became initially profitable. The month after, another 1.5x. We hit $1M ARR 6 months after niching down, and today we're at $17M ARR, still fully bootstrapped.

What I took from it:

1. Niche down to grow. After we picked lead-gen agencies & sales teams, we grew 26% MoM on avg during that early stretch.

2. Listen to your sales calls and your closed-lost deals. The calls pointed us to agencies, and after that our closed-lost deals basically built our roadmap.

3. IMO the offer is the biggest growth lever you have early on, and you won't nail it at the beginning. Launch with the price & offer that makes sense to you and listen to the market. Almost always, it will tell you what works.

Wrote the whole story down here 👇

Back in 2023, we opened up the first free beta of @heyreach_io.

More than 200 companies signed up. We gave them 30 days to try it. 126 were actively using it, getting results and telling us they loved it.

Then the beta ended, and we asked them to pay. Only one company converted.

I couldn't understand it. These companies were already getting value from the product. They'd told us that themselves. What was missing?

I was treating signups, active usage and positive feedback as proof that people would pay.

I'd decided those people would become customers.

That's an easy assumption to make when everyone keeps telling you how much they love what you're building.

So before calling a product validated, I'd want someone to buy it.

We still offer free trials at HeyReach. I want people to try the product in their own workflow before paying.

But looking back, my mistake was deciding we'd found the answer while everyone was still using it for free. I was stopping the test too soon.

Getting the payment is the next test. Then comes the work of making sure the customer gets what they paid for.

> Help them get a result.
> Find out where they get stuck.
> Talk to the people who stay and the people who leave
> Use the feedback to improve the product.
> Then try selling it again to people with the same problem.

That's the loop I mean when I talk about finding product-market fit. You keep learning from sales, usage and churn, then taking those lessons back into the product and the offer.

A good sign of PMF is also when a specific type of customer keeps using the product, gets value from it, keeps paying, and you can find more customers like them who do the same.

Until that starts repeating, I wouldn't pour money into getting signups and call it growth. I'd rather understand what happens to the people already brought in.

Before you decide LinkedIn outreach doesn't work, check these 6 things.

I think LinkedIn is one of the best ways to grow pipeline, and it gets better with cold email running next to it.

These six recommendations below are a result of studying nearly 100k campaigns that ran on @heyreach_io over the last one year (link to the full report in the replies):

1. Count how many accept, then how many of those write back

Send 100 requests and about 21 people accept. Out of those 21, about 4 write back. That's a typical campaign.

Look at those two separately, they break for different reasons.

If almost nobody accepts, the problem is usually at the targeting level or to do with your profile. Check: who you picked, how your profile looks, what the request said.

Plenty of accepts and then silence? That's the message you send after.

2. Try sending connection requests with no note at all

Blank requests got accepted 27 times out of 100. Ones with a personalized note got 22. I was sure it was the other way round.

The note does help, just later. Once they accept, a short specific line lifts replies.

Cold list, test both. People who already know you, skip it.

3. Cut the list until you can say why each person is on it

"VP Sales, US, SaaS" gives you about 4,000 people with nothing in common. "VP Sales at 11 to 50 employee SaaS companies that posted an SDR job in the last 60 days" gives you about 400.

Every list starts as a few hundred hand-picked prospects and fills up with "might as wells". Those go first.

4. Fix the profile before you touch the copy

A profile with nothing on it and 200 connections gets ignored no matter how good the connection note or the initial pitch is.

Go in this order: who you're messaging, then how your profile looks, then the copy.

5. Message them within three hours of them accepting

One agency running outreach for real-estate clients got to every new connection inside three hours. Not same day, under three hours. Their positive replies came in at 26%.

Open with the real reason you connected. Ask one question they could answer right away. No pitching right away, sending an elaborate deck, or asking for a "quick call?".

Then one follow up, three or four days later, with something they can use.

6. Go look at the best campaigns in the data

One in six gets 40 replies for every 100 conversations they start. At the very top, a recruiting campaign turned 800 connections into 571 replies in two weeks.

Completely different industries, and all of them doing the boring stuff above:

> They went narrow on who they messaged.
> The accounts doing the sending have real profiles behind them.
> And the first message makes it obvious why they're writing.

Our first Done-For-You client with him got 45 interested replies from 500 people in 4 days, 5 meetings and a closed deal... and he still won't call it a win.

If you've ever had a great first week followed by a dead month, you get why. He only trusts a result once it keeps showing up every month.

Here's what you should steal from his approach:

1. Look at the 3rd tier of your list, the buyers you'd normally get to in month 3. If that's a market you've never sold to, sneak a few messages to them in month 1 like Martin does. If they reply, you just found a new market 2 months early (and if not, you lost a few messages).

2. Swap your call ask for something they can say yes to. For a glove manufacturer, his team changed 1 sentence to "Is this the right address to send the free sample to?" Once the samples showed up, people agreed to meet (a lot of them in person) just to give feedback on the gloves.

3. Make your last follow-up name the right person: "I appreciate this might not be your call. Should I speak to {John} instead?" After that, stop. Park the lead and come back in 3 months.

4. After every booked call, ask whoever took it 3 things: was it a good meeting, was it the decision maker, and did anyone else join? Then fix your list with the answers.

5. Put every "reach out in January" or "talk to Maria instead" reply on a dated list. Tbh that's the one I'd steal first... your competitors can buy the same hiring and funding data you do, but they'll never know who told you to come back in January.

I run a SaaS and I agree with @levelsio to an extent.

"SaaS" is two completely different things now, and everyone argues about them like they're one.

Kind 1: software you use yourself. A scraper, a dashboard, a bot that scores your own leads. One user, and it only has to work when you open (or use) it.

Kind 2: software other people pay for. For eg: 7,000+ companies run their LinkedIn outreach on ours.

He's probably right about kind 1. Vibe code it. The maintenance is yours and it's kinda nothing:

- you're the only user, so nobody finds the bug before you do
- nobody paid, so nothing was promised. it can be down for a week
- it runs on your account and your laptop. no caps, no proxies, no permissions, no billing
- when it breaks, you fix it when you feel like it (or you don't)

Our first product, Howitzer, started as a Reddit DM script Stefan and I ran for ourselves. Kind 1.

The moment people paid for it, it was kind 2, and Reddit cutting DM limits completely killed it.

Now...Kind 2 only works if:

- the platform you built on changes the rules and you're still able to make things work.

LinkedIn capped everyone at ~100 invites a week and most tools in our space died. We'd been spreading volume across multiple sender accounts since day one, so it didn't kill us

- it doesn't collapse when 5x the users show up. Oct 2024 we had 1,000 customers on a product built for 200, and rewrote everything with people still using it.

- someone answers. For us that's a whole team now

- most of the roadmap is maintenance. About 70% of our dev time goes to features that already shipped, new ones get the other 30%

- other people's workflows run through it. Agencies have us wired into Clay, Instantly and Smartlead, so every change we ship has to not break any of that

Sure, the era of personal software is here, but there's far more nuance to it, than calling software or SaaS dead.

Vibe code the app, sure. Roughly what week 2 onwards looks like, for any SaaS, ours included:

- A dependency ships a breaking change and your build is red on a Tuesday for no reason
- The SSL cert expires (yes, still, in 2026)
- A DB migration that has to run on a live table while customers are hitting it
- Backups, and then testing a restore once, because a backup you never restored is a hope
- Monitoring that wakes up a human when something's down, and a human who picks up
- A third party API deprecates a version and 3 features silently stop working
- Stripe webhooks failing silently, so someone paid and didn't get access (or didn't pay and did)
- Failed cards, dunning emails, refunds, chargebacks, VAT on an invoice for a country you've never thought about
- A GDPR deletion request, and now you need to know every place that user's data lives
- A security questionnaire from a bigger customer, like 200 questions long
- Logs that grew into a cloud bill nobody is looking at
- A timezone bug that only happens for customers in Australia
- Chrome updates and your dropdown breaks
- A knowledge base that's 6 months behind the product
- An onboarding flow that made sense for the product 2 years ago
- A customer exporting all their data at 3am and timing out the whole thing
- Rotating an API key someone pasted in a Slack channel
- The "quick fix" from last year that half your customers now depend on
- Someone on call. Always.

You won't find any of this on a pricing page, and it's most of what the subscription pays for.

SaaS isn't dead. CRUD SaaS is dead, and tbh it should be.

A dashboard, an analytics page, a scheduler, a form builder... a form on top of a database with a Stripe button.

That was a business because building it took a team and some time (back in the day).

Now it takes just a couple of prompts to your AI and boom, it's done. No wonder the price of it all went to $0.

Nothing wrong with that either. Software gets cheaper to build every year and that's quite natural. AI just accelerated the extinction of a certain set of SaaS that is too simple to exist as a paid product.

The other kind of software that DOES things for you, and has to keep doing them when the platform under it changes the rules, or is built on a technical moat, is difficult to clone.

We've been building @heyreach_io on top of LinkedIn for 3+ years.

LinkedIn caps every account, counts a profile view the same as a message, and moves the caps whenever it feels like it. Get it wrong once and your customers get restrictions and the whole thing breaks. (We've had our own 3-day meltdown when usage doubled in a month, so no high horse here.)

if you are a really good signal provider and would like to be part of Loopster, email: umer@loopster.ai

also if you know any great signal providers you think we should add, share this post with them

a lot of data vendors approached us to integrate, so we decided to create a form - "Become a vendor".

we have automated most of the process, and everything is done through a short form:
1. You give us your website and email
2. Type of data you offer (emails, phones, profile data, signals, etc.)
3. How do you package your data + API RPS
4. Benchmarks of your data vs. other providers (if you have some)
5. We give you a set of data (10K leads) to enrich it and send us the result
6. You give us access with 10K credits on @UmerIshaq181's email to test it on our own dataset
7. We contact you and create a Slack connect if we decide to work together 

85% of this process is fully automated on our side (generating datasets to test, testing it, etc.), so we move really fast.

Data is becoming a commodity. It's a race to the bottom price-wise nowadays.

For example, we just came up with a solution where we can have THE FRESHEST DATA ON THE MARKET, all the time, for $70-80K/mo. 

If you are a data company that's betting only on the data that anyone has, you don't have a MOAT on the long run.

This doesn't mean that you can't sell to the 98% of the market that's still not aware of this, but I'm seeing more and more companies solving it super easily and super fast (eg: @blitzapi, LeadOcean, Moltsets, etc.).

The real MOAT is the distribution, for now. If you are a data vendor that has nailed the distribution and you are present EVERYWHERE, you'll probably win for a few more years. Because the market adopts slowly.

We live in the bubble, and you see the evangelists like Growth Engine X, Taylor, Balsa, Understory adopting these things immediately, but for the rest of the market (which is HUGE, and probably 98%), it's still "let me buy ZoomInfo/Apollo/Lusha"

The next data moat is data generated from leads' behavior.

- Is this lead more likely to reply to LinkedIn DM or an email?

- What's the phone pickup rate of this lead?

- How is this lead replying to this kind of offers?

- Which job title or industry is this lead most likely to reply to?

This change will come slowly, but it's coming for sure.
If you plan to be relevant in 3-4 years from now, you have to adapt.
